Correct. The simple past "hit" fits an event in 2003.
"Has hit" is present perfect, which connects to the present. It does not fit a single event in 2003.
"Will hit" is future tense, but the blackout already happened.
"Walk" is present tense, which shifts away from the past-tense events in the rest of the sentence.
Correct. The simple past "walked" matches "hit" and shows that the walking happened after the blackout and after the subways had stopped.
"Have walked" is present perfect, which does not fit a story set in 2003.
"Had walked" would mean the commuters walked home before the blackout hit, which makes no sense.

questions.solutionExplanation: The sentence describes a past event, so both blanks need past tense verbs: "When the blackout of 2003 hit New York City, thousands of commuters walked across the bridges." The past perfect "had stopped" is already in the sentence to show that the subways stopped before the walk began. The walking itself should be in the simple past.
questions.commonTrap: Students who see "had stopped" may choose "had walked" to match it. But the past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions. The subways stopped first and the commuters walked second, so "walked" is correct.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the options that correctly complete the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct word for each blank.

segments.value: Over the summer, the soccer
locker room was repainted, and
new benches arrived just before the first home game.

options.explanation: Correct. The locker room belongs to one team, so the singular possessive is "team's."
"Teams" is a plural noun with no apostrophe, so it does not show that the locker room belongs to the team.
"Teams'" is the plural possessive, which would mean the locker room belongs to several teams. The sentence refers to one soccer team.
"It's" means "it is." "It is new benches arrived" makes no sense.
Correct. "Its" is the possessive pronoun, showing that the new benches belong to the locker room.
"Its'" is not a word. The possessive pronoun "its" never takes an apostrophe.

questions.solutionExplanation: In the first blank, the locker room belongs to one soccer team, so the singular possessive "team's" is correct. In the second blank, the benches belong to the locker room. Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes, so the correct word is "its."
questions.commonTrap: Students often choose "it's" because they know apostrophes show possession. But "it's" always means "it is" or "it has." Possessive pronouns such as "its," "hers," and "theirs" have no apostrophe.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the option that correctly completes the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct punctuation and transition for the blank.

segments.value: The neighborhood library had planned to reopen in
the repairs took longer than expected, so the doors stayed closed until June.

options.explanation: This creates a comma splice. "However" is a transition word, not a conjunction, so commas alone cannot join two complete sentences.
Correct. The semicolon ends the first complete sentence, and the comma after "however" sets off the transition at the start of the second.
With no punctuation before "however," the two complete sentences run together. This is a run-on.
The semicolon after "however" is wrong. "However" is not a complete sentence, so it cannot stand between two semicolons.

questions.solutionExplanation: "The neighborhood library had planned to reopen in March" is a complete sentence, and so is "the repairs took longer than expected, so the doors stayed closed until June." When "however" begins the second sentence, the first must end with a semicolon or a period, and a comma follows "however." The correct choice is "March; however,".
questions.commonTrap: "March, however," is the trap. Students see "however" set off by commas in many correct sentences, where it interrupts a single clause. Here it comes between two complete sentences, so a semicolon is required before it.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the option that correctly completes the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct punctuation for the blank.

segments.value: Before the hike, Ms. Patel reminded us to pack three
water, sunscreen, and a map of the trail.

options.explanation: A semicolon must join two complete sentences. "Water, sunscreen, and a map of the trail" is a list, not a sentence.
A comma makes "three essentials" look like one more item in the list, so a reader might count four items instead of three.
Correct. "Before the hike, Ms. Patel reminded us to pack three essentials" is a complete sentence, so a colon can introduce the list that names the essentials.
A colon cannot follow "such as," because "such as" cannot end a complete sentence. "Such as" also suggests these are only some examples, but the sentence names exactly three essentials.

questions.solutionExplanation: A colon introduces a list or explanation after a complete sentence. The words before the blank form a complete sentence and announce "three essentials," and the words after it name them. A colon is the correct choice.
questions.commonTrap: Students who are unsure of colons may pick the comma because commas appear throughout lists. But a comma here blurs the line between the announcement and the list itself.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the options that correctly complete the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct words and punctuation for each blank.

segments.value: The
first opened at Coney Island in
still one of the most famous wooden roller coasters in the world.

options.explanation: Correct. There is only one Cyclone, so the "which" clause adds extra information and must begin with a comma.
Leaving out the comma treats the clause as if it were needed to tell which Cyclone is meant. Since the name already identifies the ride, the clause is extra and needs commas.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. "The Cyclone" by itself is not a sentence.
Without a closing comma, the extra clause never ends, and the main verb "is" seems to belong to the clause.
Correct. The comma closes the "which" clause, so the main sentence reads "The Cyclone is still one of the most famous wooden roller coasters."
A semicolon cannot separate the subject "The Cyclone" from its verb "is."

questions.solutionExplanation: The clause "which first opened at Coney Island in 1927" adds extra information about the Cyclone. Because it interrupts the main sentence, "The Cyclone is still one of the most famous wooden roller coasters in the world," it needs a comma on each side. The correct choices are "Cyclone, which" and "1927, is."
questions.commonTrap: Many students choose the opening comma correctly but forget the closing one, because the comma before "is" seems to separate a subject from its verb. Here the comma closes the interrupting clause, so it is required.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the options that correctly complete the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct pronoun for each blank.

segments.value: Coach Delgado,
had watched us practice all week, asked Maya and
to lead the warm-up before the championship game.

options.explanation: "Whom" is an object pronoun. Here the pronoun does the watching, so it is a subject.
Correct. "Who" is the subject of "had watched," so the subject form is needed.
"Which" refers to things or animals, not people. Coach Delgado is a person.
"I" is a subject pronoun. The coach asked Maya and the writer, so the pronoun is an object. Test it: "asked I" is wrong.
Correct. "Me" is the object of "asked." Removing "Maya and" gives "asked me," which is correct.
"Myself" is used only when the subject of the sentence is "I." The subject here is Coach Delgado.

questions.solutionExplanation: In the first blank, the pronoun is the subject of "had watched," and it refers to a person, so "who" is correct. In the second blank, the pronoun receives the action of "asked," so it must be the object pronoun "me."
questions.commonTrap: Students often choose "Maya and I" because it sounds formal. Drop "Maya and" and test the pronoun alone. "The coach asked I" is clearly wrong.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the options that correctly complete the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct word for each blank.

segments.value: City officials hope the new flood walls will
damage from future storms, but critics say the project's
on nearby neighborhoods has not been carefully studied.

options.explanation: "Deduce" means to figure something out by reasoning. Flood walls cannot figure out damage.
Correct. "Reduce" means to make smaller, which is what flood walls are meant to do to storm damage.
"Produce" means to create. Officials would not hope that flood walls create damage.
"Affect" is almost always a verb meaning "to influence." The blank follows "the project's" and needs a noun.
"Effort" means hard work or an attempt. "The project's effort on nearby neighborhoods" does not make sense.
Correct. "Effect" is a noun meaning "result." The critics are concerned about the project's result on nearby neighborhoods.

questions.solutionExplanation: The first blank needs a verb that means "make smaller," so "reduce" is correct. The second blank follows the possessive "the project's," so it needs a noun. "Effect" is the noun that means "result." "Affect" is usually a verb.
questions.commonTrap: "Affect" and "effect" are often confused. A quick test: if the word follows "the," "a," or a possessive like "the project's," it is a noun, so use "effect."

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the option that correctly completes the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct option for the blank.

segments.value: The subway was delayed for almost an
arrived at the concert just as the band began to play.

options.explanation: This joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
Correct. The comma and the conjunction "so" correctly join the two complete sentences and show that the delay caused the late arrival.
This runs two complete sentences together with no punctuation or conjunction, which is a run-on.
The comma belongs before "so," not after it. Without a comma before "so," the two sentences are not correctly joined.

questions.solutionExplanation: "The subway was delayed for almost an hour" and "we arrived at the concert just as the band began to play" are both complete sentences. To join them, use a comma followed by a conjunction. "So" shows that the delay caused the late arrival, so "hour, so we" is correct.
questions.commonTrap: "Hour, we" is tempting because a comma marks the natural pause. But a pause is not enough to join two complete sentences. A conjunction such as "so" is required.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Select the options that correctly complete the sentence.

ic.instruction: Choose the correct verb for each blank.

segments.value: Neither the art teacher nor her students
sure where the new mural will go, but each of the three proposed walls
enough space for a design twenty feet wide.

options.explanation: "Is" agrees with "the art teacher," but with "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it, "her students."
Correct. With "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "Her students" is plural, so the verb is "are."
"Was" is singular and past tense. It does not agree with "her students," and it does not fit the present and future tenses used in the rest of the sentence.
"Have" agrees with "walls," but "walls" is inside a prepositional phrase. The subject is "each," which is singular.
Correct. The subject is "each," which is singular, so the verb is "has." "Walls" is part of the phrase "of the three proposed walls" and is not the subject.
"Having" is an -ing form that cannot be a main verb by itself, so the second half of the sentence would have no verb.

questions.solutionExplanation: The sentence has two agreement problems. In the first clause, "neither ... nor" joins a singular subject and a plural subject, and the verb agrees with the nearer one, "her students," so the verb is "are." In the second clause, the subject is "each," which is always singular, so the verb is "has."
questions.commonTrap: The plural "walls" sits right before the second blank, which pulls students toward "have." Cross out "of the three proposed walls" and the subject "each" is left, which needs "has."
